- Works **after** services like **GuardDuty**, **Macie**, and **Security Hub** detect potential threats.

documents.title: Security & Compliance: Problem It Solves
documents.content:
### Problem It Solves

- Security findings often need **deeper analysis** to understand _how_ and _why_ they happened.
- This analysis can be **complex**, **time-consuming**, and involve **correlating data** from multiple sources.

documents.title: Security & Compliance: How It Works
documents.content:
### How It Works

- Uses **Machine Learning (ML)** and **graph-based analysis** to:
- Connect related events and entities automatically.
- Show visual relationships to **quickly pinpoint the root cause**.

documents.title: Security & Compliance: Data Sources
documents.content:
### Data Sources

Amazon Detective automatically collects and processes data from:

- **VPC Flow Logs** (network traffic)
- **AWS CloudTrail** (API calls)
- **Amazon GuardDuty** (threat detection)

documents.title: Security & Compliance: Output
documents.content:
### Output

- Provides **visualizations and context** for incidents.
- Gives a **unified view** of security-related data.
- Helps you understand **who did what, when, and from where**.

documents.title: Security & Compliance: Key Idea
documents.content:
### Key Idea

> Amazon Detective doesn’t detect issues; it helps you **investigate and understand them**.

documents.title: Security & Compliance: AWS Abuse Reporting
documents.content:
## AWS Abuse Reporting
---

documents.title: Security & Compliance: Purpose
documents.content:
### Purpose

- To **report abusive or illegal activities** happening through AWS resources.

documents.title: Security & Compliance: When to Report
documents.content:
### When to Report

You should contact the **AWS Abuse Team** if you notice:

- **Spam** emails coming from AWS-owned IPs
- **Spam** on websites or forums using AWS resources
- **Port scanning** activity from AWS servers
- **DDoS (Distributed Denial of Service)** attacks
- **Intrusion attempts** on your systems from AWS IPs
- **Hosting of illegal or copyrighted content** on AWS
- **Distribution of malware** from AWS infrastructure

documents.title: Security & Compliance: How to Report
documents.content:
### How to Report

You can report abuse in two ways:

1. **Online form** (available on AWS Abuse page)
2. **Email**: 📧 **[abuse@amazonaws.com](mailto:abuse@amazonaws.com)**

documents.title: Security & Compliance: Exam Tip
documents.content:
### Exam Tip

> For the AWS exam, just remember:
> If you suspect abuse or illegal activity from AWS resources, **email the AWS Abuse Team** at
> ➡️ **[abuse@amazonaws.com](mailto:abuse@amazonaws.com)**

documents.title: Security & Compliance: AWS Root User Privileges
documents.content:
## AWS Root User Privileges
---

documents.title: Security & Compliance: What is the Root User?
documents.content:
### What is the Root User?

- The **Root User** is the **original account owner** created when an AWS account is first made.
- It has **full, unrestricted access** to **all AWS services and resources**.

documents.title: Security & Compliance: Best Practice
documents.content:
### Best Practice

- **Never use the root account** for daily or administrative tasks.
- **Create an IAM user** with admin privileges instead.
- **Secure the root account credentials** (especially the secret access keys).
- **Enable MFA** (Multi-Factor Authentication) on the root account.

documents.title: Security & Compliance: Actions Only the Root User Can Perform
documents.content:
### Actions Only the Root User Can Perform

These are **exclusive to the root user** and may appear on the exam:

1. **Account Management**
- Change **account name**, **root email**, **root password**, or **root access keys**.
- View **certain tax invoices**.
- **Close the AWS account**.
2. **IAM and Permissions**
- **Restore IAM user permissions** if permissions are accidentally removed.
3. **Support Plans**
- **Change or cancel** your AWS Support plan.
4. **Reserved Instance Marketplace**
- **Register as a seller** in the **Reserved Instance Marketplace**.
_(Example: If you bought a 3-year Reserved Instance but don’t need it after 2 years, you can resell it — only the root user can register as a seller.)_
5. **Amazon S3**
- **Enable MFA Delete** on an S3 bucket.
- **Edit or delete bucket policies** that contain **invalid VPC IDs or endpoint IDs**.
6. **AWS GovCloud**
- **Sign up for AWS GovCloud**.

documents.title: Security & Compliance: Exam Tip
documents.content:
### Exam Tip

> Remember: **Root user = full control**, but **should only be used for rare, account-level operations** like closing the account or changing billing details.

documents.title: Security & Compliance: IAM Access Analyzer (AWS)
documents.content:
## IAM Access Analyzer (AWS)
---

documents.title: Security & Compliance: Purpose
documents.content:
### Purpose

- Helps **identify AWS resources shared externally** (outside your AWS account or organization).
- Detects **potential unintended access** to your resources.
- Built into the **IAM console** and **free to use**.

documents.title: Security & Compliance: Resources it Analyzes
documents.content:
### Resources it Analyzes

IAM Access Analyzer checks these for external sharing:

- **S3 Buckets**
- **IAM Roles**
- **KMS Keys**
- **Lambda Functions and Layers**
- **SQS Queues**
- **Secrets Manager Secrets**

documents.title: Security & Compliance: Concept of Zone of Trust
documents.content:
### Concept of Zone of Trust

- Defines what’s considered **“internal”** or **trusted**.
- Can be:
- Your **AWS account**, or
- Your **AWS Organization** (all accounts under it).
- Anything **outside** this zone is **flagged** as a **finding**.

documents.title: Security & Compliance: How It Works
documents.content:
### How It Works

1. **You create an analyzer** in the IAM console.
- Example name: `console-analyzer`.
- Choose zone of trust (usually current account).
- Optionally, add tags.
2. It **creates a service-linked role** to scan your resources.
3. **Findings** show resources shared externally.

documents.title: Security & Compliance: Example
documents.content:
### Example

Suppose you have an **S3 bucket** or **SQS queue** shared:

- With **another AWS account**,
- With **an external client**,
- With **all principals** (`*`),
- Or through an **open bucket policy**.

If it’s **outside your zone of trust**, Access Analyzer reports it.

documents.title: Security & Compliance: Managing Findings
documents.content:
### Managing Findings

Findings can have different **statuses**:

- **Active** – Currently shared externally.
- **Resolved** – Fixed (no longer shared).
- **Archived** – Intended sharing; ignored in future scans.

documents.title: Security & Compliance: Example Workflow
documents.content:
### Example Workflow

1. Analyzer finds **3 findings**:
- 1 SQS queue
- 2 S3 buckets
1. You check the **SQS policy**, see that it allows `SendMessage` from anyone (`*`).
2. You **edit or remove** that policy.
3. **Rescan** → Status becomes **Resolved**.
4. For intended public buckets, you **archive** them.

documents.title: Security & Compliance: Automation
documents.content:
### Automation

- You can create **Archive Rules** to automatically mark specific types of findings (e.g., public S3 buckets) as archived.

documents.title: Security & Compliance: Key Benefits
documents.content:
### Key Benefits

- **Improves security visibility**
- **Reduces misconfigurations**
- **Helps ensure least privilege access**

documents.title: Security & Compliance: Exam Tip / Interview Notes
documents.content:
### Exam Tip / Interview Notes

- **IAM Access Analyzer** uses **resource-based policies** to identify external access.
- **Zone of Trust** = trusted boundary (account or organization).
- **Findings** are based on **policy analysis**, not actual usage.
- It’s **free**, **automated**, and **available in IAM console**.

documents.title: Security & Compliance: AWS Security & Compliance — Summary Notes
documents.content:
## AWS Security & Compliance — Summary Notes
---

documents.title: Security & Compliance: Shared Responsibility Model
documents.content:
### Shared Responsibility Model

- **AWS** is responsible for **security _of_ the cloud** (infrastructure, hardware, global network).
- **You (the customer)** are responsible for **security _in_ the cloud** (data, configuration, identity management).

documents.title: Security & Compliance: AWS Shield
documents.content:
### AWS Shield

- **Automatic DDoS protection** service.
- **Shield Standard:** Free, automatic protection.
- **Shield Advanced:** Paid version with
- 24/7 DDoS response team (DRT) access
- Additional analytics and cost protection.

documents.title: Security & Compliance: AWS WAF (Web Application Firewall)
documents.content:
### AWS WAF (Web Application Firewall)

- Protects web applications from **common attacks** like SQL injection and XSS.
- Filters incoming HTTP(S) requests based on **custom rules**.

documents.title: Security & Compliance: AWS KMS (Key Management Service)
documents.content:
### AWS KMS (Key Management Service)

- **Manages encryption keys** for your AWS resources.
- **AWS manages the hardware & keys** (customer controls usage and permissions).

documents.title: Security & Compliance: AWS CloudHSM (Hardware Security Module)
documents.content:
### AWS CloudHSM (Hardware Security Module)

- Provides **hardware-based encryption**.
- **Customer manages the keys**, AWS only manages the physical device.
- Used for **compliance or regulatory needs** requiring full control over keys.

documents.title: Security & Compliance: AWS Certificate Manager (ACM)
documents.content:
### AWS Certificate Manager (ACM)

- **Provisions, manages, and deploys SSL/TLS certificates**.
- Used for **in-flight encryption** (data encrypted while being transmitted).

documents.title: Security & Compliance: AWS Artifact
documents.content:
### AWS Artifact

- Central location for **AWS compliance reports** and **agreements** (PCI DSS, ISO, SOC reports, etc.).
- Useful for audits and documentation.

documents.title: Security & Compliance: AWS GuardDuty
documents.content:
### AWS GuardDuty

- **Threat detection service** that identifies malicious or unauthorized activity.
- Analyzes:
- **VPC Flow Logs**
- **DNS Logs**
- **CloudTrail Logs**

documents.title: Security & Compliance: AWS Inspector
documents.content:
### AWS Inspector

- **Vulnerability scanning service** for:
- EC2 instances
- ECR container images
- Lambda functions
- Detects software vulnerabilities and network exposures.

documents.title: Security & Compliance: AWS Network Firewall
documents.content:
### AWS Network Firewall

- Protects **VPCs from network-level attacks**.
- Allows configuration of **stateful** and **stateless** rule groups.

documents.title: Security & Compliance: AWS Config
documents.content:
### AWS Config

- Tracks **configuration changes** over time.
- Helps with **auditing** and **compliance** by defining **config rules** to evaluate resource compliance.

documents.title: Security & Compliance: AWS Macie
documents.content:
### AWS Macie

- Uses **machine learning** to discover and protect **sensitive data** in S3 (like PII, credit card info, etc.).

documents.title: Security & Compliance: AWS CloudTrail
documents.content:
### AWS CloudTrail

- Logs all **API calls** and **user activity** in your account.
- Essential for **auditing** and **security investigation**.

documents.title: Security & Compliance: AWS Security Hub
documents.content:
### AWS Security Hub

- **Centralizes security findings** from multiple AWS services (GuardDuty, Inspector, Macie, etc.) across multiple accounts.
- Provides **security score** and **recommended remediations**.

documents.title: Security & Compliance: AWS Detective
documents.content:
### AWS Detective

- Helps **analyze and investigate** security incidents to find the **root cause**.
- Correlates logs and findings from multiple services (like GuardDuty and CloudTrail).

documents.title: Security & Compliance: AWS Abuse Team
documents.content:
### AWS Abuse Team

- Report **abusive or illegal activity** using AWS resources.
- Contact via **form or email**.

documents.title: Security & Compliance: Root User Privileges
documents.content:
### Root User Privileges

A root user can:

1. Change **account settings**.
2. **Close** AWS account.
3. **Change or cancel** support plan.
4. **Register as a seller** in the Reserved Instances Marketplace.

_(Always secure the root account with MFA and avoid daily use.)_

documents.title: Security & Compliance: IAM Access Analyzer
documents.content:
### IAM Access Analyzer

- Identifies **resources shared externally** (outside your “zone of trust”).
- Analyzes **resource-based policies** to detect public or cross-account access.

documents.title: Security & Compliance: AWS Firewall Manager
documents.content:
### AWS Firewall Manager

- **Centralized security management** for your organization.
- Manages:
- **Security Groups**
- **WAF**
- **Shield Advanced policies**
- Ensures **consistent rules** across multiple accounts.

documents.title: Security & Compliance: Key Takeaways
documents.content:
### Key Takeaways

- AWS provides **many security tools**, but **you** must configure them correctly.
- Focus on **monitoring (GuardDuty, CloudTrail)**, **protection (Shield, WAF, Network Firewall)**, and **compliance (Config, Artifact)**.
- **Security Hub** is your **central dashboard** for all findings.

documents.title: VPC & Networking
documents.content:
VPC & Networking
AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner notes on VPC & Networking
Read: https://ahmadx.dev/posts/aws-ccp-vpc-networking/

documents.title: VPC & Networking: VPC & Networking (Overview)
documents.content:
## VPC & Networking (Overview)
---

documents.title: VPC & Networking: What is a VPC?
documents.content:
### What is a VPC?

- **VPC (Virtual Private Cloud)** is a **private, isolated section** of the AWS cloud where you can launch and manage your AWS resources (like EC2, RDS, etc.).
- It provides **control over networking**, including IP addressing, subnets, routing, and security.
- Think of it as your own **virtual data center** in AWS.

documents.title: VPC & Networking: Why VPC Matters
documents.content:
### Why VPC Matters

- VPC concepts are essential for networking-related AWS services.
- **In-depth knowledge** is required for advanced certifications such as:
- AWS Certified **Solutions Architect – Associate**
- AWS Certified **SysOps Administrator – Associate**
- For **CCP**, understanding **high-level concepts** and their **purpose** is sufficient.

documents.title: VPC & Networking: Key Components to Know (for CCP)
documents.content:
### Key Components to Know (for CCP)

|**Component**|**Purpose / Function**|
|---|---|
|**VPC**|The virtual private network environment in AWS.|
|**Subnets**|Divide a VPC into smaller networks; can be **public** (internet-accessible) or **private**.|
|**Internet Gateway (IGW)**|Allows communication between resources in a **public subnet** and the **internet**.|
|**NAT Gateway**|Enables **outbound internet access** for **private subnets** without exposing them publicly.|
|**Security Groups**|Act as **stateful firewalls** controlling inbound and outbound traffic **at the instance level**.|
|**Network ACLs (NACLs)**|**Stateless firewalls** controlling traffic **at the subnet level**.|
|**VPC Flow Logs**|Capture **network traffic information** for monitoring and troubleshooting.|
|**VPC Peering**|Connects **two VPCs privately** using AWS’s internal network.|
|**VPC Endpoints**|Enable **private connectivity** to AWS services (like S3, DynamoDB) without using the internet.|
|**Site-to-Site VPN**|Connects an **on-premises network** to a **VPC** over the internet securely.|
|**Direct Connect**|Establishes a **dedicated physical connection** between on-premises and AWS for low latency.|
|**Transit Gateway**|Central hub to **connect multiple VPCs and on-premises networks** efficiently.|

documents.title: VPC & Networking: CCP Exam Relevance
documents.content:
### CCP Exam Relevance

- The **VPC topic** accounts for **less than 1–2 questions** on the exam.
- Focus on **definitions, purposes, and relationships** between components.
- Hands-on familiarity with the **default VPC** (created automatically by AWS) is helpful.

documents.title: VPC & Networking: Key Takeaways
documents.content:
### Key Takeaways

- Understand what each component **does** and **why it’s used**.
- No need to configure or design a VPC for the CCP level.
- Exam tests **conceptual clarity**, not technical implementation.

documents.title: VPC & Networking: IP Addresses in AWS
documents.content:
## IP Addresses in AWS
---

documents.title: VPC & Networking: IPv4 Overview
documents.content:
### IPv4 Overview

- **IPv4** (Internet Protocol version 4) provides around **4.3 billion unique addresses**.
- Common format: `192.0.2.1` (four octets).
- Used for **most existing networks and devices**.

documents.title: VPC & Networking: Public IPv4
documents.content:
### Public IPv4

- **Public IPs** are **reachable over the internet**.
- Assigned automatically when creating EC2 instances (if enabled).
- **Behavior**:
- Released when instance is **stopped**.
- A **new public IP** is assigned when instance is **started again**.
- **Pricing**:
- AWS charges **$0.005/hour** per public IPv4 address (including Elastic IPs).
- **Free Tier**: 750 hours of public IPv4 usage per month.

documents.title: VPC & Networking: Private IPv4
documents.content:
### Private IPv4

- Used for **internal communication** within private networks (e.g., inside a VPC).
- Example range: `192.168.0.0/16`.
- **Not accessible from the internet**.
- **Remains the same** for an EC2 instance’s entire lifetime, even after stop/start.

documents.title: VPC & Networking: Elastic IP (EIP)
documents.content:
### Elastic IP (EIP)

- A **static public IPv4 address** that remains the same even if an instance is stopped and restarted.
- Useful for **consistent IP mapping** (e.g., DNS records).
- **Charged** if allocated but **not associated** with a running instance.

documents.title: VPC & Networking: IPv6 Overview
documents.content:
### IPv6 Overview

- **IPv6** (Internet Protocol version 6) is the **newer protocol** with **3.4 × 10³⁸ addresses** (virtually unlimited).
- Example format: `2600:1f18:abcd:1234::1`.
- **All IPv6 addresses are public** (no private range).
- **Free to use** in AWS (no hourly charge).

documents.title: VPC & Networking: IPv4 vs IPv6 (Quick Comparison)
documents.content:
### IPv4 vs IPv6 (Quick Comparison)

|Feature|**IPv4**|**IPv6**|
|---|---|---|
|Address Space|4.3 billion|3.4 × 10³⁸|
|Format|4 decimal octets (e.g., 192.168.0.1)|Hexadecimal blocks (e.g., 2600:1f18::1)|
|Private Range|Yes|No|
|Internet Reachability|Optional|Always Public|
|AWS Cost|$0.005/hour|Free|
|Example Usage|Legacy systems, internal networking|New apps, scalable internet exposure|

documents.title: VPC & Networking: Exam Tip
documents.content:
### Exam Tip

- Know the difference between **public**, **private**, and **elastic** IPs.
- Remember: **IPv6 = free + public-only + huge address space**.
- For CCP, focus on **behavior and cost**, not configuration details.

documents.title: VPC & Networking: VPC (Virtual Private Cloud) Overview
documents.content:
## VPC (Virtual Private Cloud) Overview
---

documents.title: VPC & Networking: Definition
documents.content:
### Definition

- **VPC (Virtual Private Cloud)** is a **private, isolated network** in AWS used to **deploy cloud resources** like EC2 instances, databases, etc.
- Each **VPC is region-specific**.
- If you use multiple AWS Regions, you have **separate VPCs** in each region.

documents.title: VPC & Networking: VPC Structure
documents.content:
### VPC Structure

- A VPC contains **subnets**, which are **partitions** of the VPC network.
- Each **subnet** is associated with **one Availability Zone (AZ)**.
- **CIDR Range (Classless Inter-Domain Routing)** defines the **IP address range** of a VPC. Example: `10.0.0.0/16`.

documents.title: VPC & Networking: Subnets
documents.content:
### Subnets

| **Type** | **Description** | **Typical Use** |
| ------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Public Subnet** | Has direct access to the internet through an **Internet Gateway (IGW)**. | EC2 instances that need to be reachable from the internet, Load Balancers. |
| **Private Subnet** | **No direct access** from the internet. Can still access the internet indirectly (via NAT). | Databases, backend servers, internal applications. |

- **Subnets are made public** when their route tables include a route to an Internet Gateway.

documents.title: VPC & Networking: Route Tables
documents.content:
### Route Tables

- **Route Tables** define how traffic flows **between subnets** and **to external networks**.
- **Public subnet route** → Internet Gateway (IGW).
- **Private subnet route** → NAT Gateway or NAT Instance (for outbound internet access).

documents.title: VPC & Networking: Internet Gateway (IGW)
documents.content:
### Internet Gateway (IGW)

- A **managed AWS component** that allows communication **between VPC and the internet**.
- Must be **attached to a VPC**.
- Used by **public subnets** for inbound/outbound internet access.

documents.title: VPC & Networking: NAT Gateway / NAT Instance
documents.content:
### NAT Gateway / NAT Instance

|**Feature**|**NAT Gateway (Managed)**|**NAT Instance (Self-managed)**|
|---|---|---|
|**Purpose**|Allows **private subnet instances** to access the internet **outbound only**.|Same purpose, but requires user maintenance.|
|**Location**|Must be in a **public subnet**.|Must be in a **public subnet**.|
|**Inbound Access**|Not allowed from the internet.|Not allowed (by default).|
|**Use Case**|Update servers, download patches, access external APIs.|Custom configurations.|

**Flow Example:**
Private subnet → NAT Gateway → Internet Gateway → Internet

documents.title: VPC & Networking: Multi-AZ VPC Example
documents.content:
### Multi-AZ VPC Example

- Example layout:
- **Region** → contains one **VPC**
- **VPC** → spans **two AZs**
- **Each AZ** → has one **public** and one **private** subnet
- **Total:** 1 VPC, 2 AZs, 4 Subnets (2 public + 2 private)
- EC2 instances can be deployed in any subnet.

documents.title: VPC & Networking: Key Exam Tips
documents.content:
### Key Exam Tips

- **VPC = isolated private network in AWS.**
- **Public subnet = has route to Internet Gateway.**
- **Private subnet = no direct internet route.**
- **NAT Gateway = outbound internet for private subnets only.**
- **Internet Gateway = inbound/outbound internet access for public subnets.**
- **VPCs are region-scoped**, **subnets are AZ-scoped**.

documents.title: VPC & Networking: Network Security in VPC
documents.content:
## Network Security in VPC
---

documents.title: VPC & Networking: Two Main Security Layers
documents.content:
### Two Main Security Layers

1. **Network ACL (NACL)** — subnet-level firewall
2. **Security Group (SG)** — instance-level firewall

These work **together** to secure traffic _to and from_ your EC2 instances inside a VPC.

documents.title: VPC & Networking: Network ACL (NACL)
documents.content: ### Network ACL (NACL)

documents.title: VPC & Networking: Definition
documents.content:
#### Definition

- A **firewall that operates at the subnet level**.
- Controls **inbound and outbound traffic** for subnets.
- Rules are **evaluated in order**, starting from the lowest rule number.

documents.title: VPC & Networking: Characteristics
documents.content:
#### Characteristics

|**Feature**|**Description**|
|---|---|
|**Scope**|Subnet-level|
|**Rules**|Can **ALLOW** or **DENY** traffic|
|**Direction**|Separate inbound and outbound rules|
|**Statefulness**|**Stateless** — return traffic must be explicitly allowed|
|**Default NACL**|Allows all inbound and outbound traffic|
|**Custom NACLs**|Start with _DENY ALL_ rules (must explicitly allow)|
|**Rules use**|Only **IP addresses** (no SG references)|

documents.title: VPC & Networking: Example
documents.content:
#### Example

- A subnet has a NACL allowing only **HTTPS (443)** inbound and outbound.
- All other ports/traffic are **denied** by default.

documents.title: VPC & Networking: Exam Tip
documents.content:
#### Exam Tip

- **NACL = stateless, subnet-level, can ALLOW or DENY.**

documents.title: VPC & Networking: Security Groups (SG)
documents.content: ### Security Groups (SG)

documents.title: VPC & Networking: **Definition**
documents.content:
#### **Definition**

- A **firewall that operates at the instance level (ENI level)**.
- Controls traffic **to and from EC2 instances**.

documents.title: VPC & Networking: Characteristics
documents.content:
#### Characteristics

|**Feature**|**Description**|
|---|---|
|**Scope**|Instance-level|
|**Rules**|**ALLOW only** (no DENY rules)|
|**Direction**|Separate inbound and outbound rules|
|**Statefulness**|**Stateful** — return traffic automatically allowed|
|**References**|Can reference **IP addresses** or **other security groups**|
|**Default SG**|Allows **no inbound**, but **all outbound** traffic|

documents.title: VPC & Networking: Example
documents.content:
#### Example

- Allow inbound **SSH (22)** from your IP.
- Allow inbound **HTTP (80)** from anywhere.
- Automatically allows responses (stateful).

documents.title: VPC & Networking: Exam Tip
documents.content:
#### Exam Tip

- **Security Group = stateful, instance-level, ALLOW-only.**

documents.title: VPC & Networking: NACL vs Security Group (Comparison)
documents.content:
### NACL vs Security Group (Comparison)

|**Feature**|**Network ACL (NACL)**|**Security Group (SG)**|
|---|---|---|
|**Scope**|Subnet-level|Instance-level|
|**Rules**|ALLOW & DENY|ALLOW only|
|**Statefulness**|Stateless|Stateful|
|**Return Traffic**|Must be explicitly allowed|Automatically allowed|
|**References**|IP addresses only|IPs or other SGs|
|**Default Behavior**|Allows all|Denies all inbound, allows all outbound|

documents.title: VPC & Networking: Default Behavior in AWS
documents.content:
### Default Behavior in AWS

- Every **VPC** automatically comes with a **default NACL** and **default SG**.
- **Default NACL** → allows **all inbound/outbound traffic**.
- **Default SG** → allows **all outbound**, **no inbound** unless specified.

documents.title: VPC & Networking: Practical Example (from AWS Console)
documents.content:
### Practical Example (from AWS Console)

- Navigate to **VPC > Security > Security Groups** to view existing groups.
- Each SG shows its **inbound and outbound rules**.
- Navigate to **VPC > Security > Network ACLs** to view subnet-level ACLs.
- Each NACL is associated with one or more **subnets**.

documents.title: VPC & Networking: Summary for Exam
documents.content:
### Summary for Exam

**NACL** → subnet-level, ALLOW/DENY, stateless, IP-based
**Security Group** → instance-level, ALLOW-only, stateful, can reference SGs
**Return traffic** → automatic for SG, manual for NACL
**Default NACL** → allows all, **Default SG** → allows outbound only

documents.title: VPC & Networking: VPC Flow Logs
documents.content:
## VPC Flow Logs
---

**Definition:**
VPC Flow Logs capture information about IP traffic going to and from network interfaces in your VPC.

**Levels of Flow Logs:**

- **VPC Flow Log** (entire VPC)
- **Subnet Flow Log** (specific subnet)
- **ENI Flow Log** (specific Elastic Network Interface, e.g., EC2)

**Purpose:**

- Monitor and troubleshoot connectivity issues:
- Subnet not connecting to the Internet
- Subnet-to-subnet connectivity problems
- Internet unable to reach a subnet
- Analyze traffic for EC2, Load Balancers, RDS, Aurora, ElastiCache, etc.

**Destinations (where logs are sent):**

- **Amazon CloudWatch Logs**
- **Amazon S3**
- **Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose**

**Configuration Options:**

- **Filter:**
- All traffic
- Accepted traffic
- Rejected traffic
- **Aggregation Interval:**
- 1 minute or 10 minutes
- **Log Format Fields:**
Version, Account ID, Interface ID, Source & Destination IPs, Ports, Protocol, Packets, Bytes, Start/End time, Action, Log status

documents.title: VPC & Networking: VPC Peering
documents.content:
### VPC Peering

**Definition:**
VPC Peering allows two VPCs to communicate privately using AWS’s internal network.

**Behavior:**

- The two VPCs behave as if they are part of the same network.
- Useful for interconnecting workloads across different VPCs, accounts, or regions.

**Key Rules:**

1. **No overlapping CIDR blocks** allowed between the VPCs.
2. **Not transitive:**
- If A↔B and A↔C are connected, **B and C cannot talk** unless you also create **B↔C** peering.
3. **Traffic routing:**
- Update route tables in both VPCs to allow communication.

**Cross-region / cross-account peering:**
Possible between VPCs in the same or different regions/accounts (requires acceptance by the other VPC owner).

documents.title: VPC & Networking: Exam Tips
documents.content:
### Exam Tips

- **Flow Logs** = Monitor traffic, find connectivity issues.
- **Peering** = Private connection between non-overlapping VPCs, not transitive.
- **Flow Logs destinations** = S3, CloudWatch, Firehose.
- **Flow Logs levels** = VPC, Subnet, ENI.

documents.title: VPC & Networking: VPC Endpoints (Private Access to AWS Services)
documents.content:
## VPC Endpoints (Private Access to AWS Services)
---

documents.title: VPC & Networking: **Concept**
documents.content:
#### **Concept**

- Normally, AWS services are accessed **publicly** via the internet.
- **VPC Endpoints** allow **private access** to AWS services within the **AWS network**, avoiding the public internet.

documents.title: VPC & Networking: **Benefits**
documents.content:
#### **Benefits**

- **Better Security** – no public internet exposure.
- **Lower Latency** – traffic stays within the AWS backbone.

documents.title: VPC & Networking: Types of VPC Endpoints
documents.content: ### Types of VPC Endpoints

documents.title: VPC & Networking: Gateway Endpoint
documents.content:
#### Gateway Endpoint

- Used **only** for:
- **Amazon S3**
- **Amazon DynamoDB**
- Traffic to these services flows privately through the **gateway**.
- **Configured at the route table level** of your VPC/subnet.

🗝️ **Remember:**
👉 _Gateway Endpoint = S3 + DynamoDB only_

documents.title: VPC & Networking: Interface Endpoint (PrivateLink)
documents.content:
#### Interface Endpoint (PrivateLink)

- Used for **most other AWS services**, for example:
- CloudWatch
- EC2
- SSM
- SNS, SQS, etc.
- Creates an **Elastic Network Interface (ENI)** in your subnet that connects privately to the service.

🗝️ **Remember:**
👉 _Interface Endpoint = For all other services (via PrivateLink)_

documents.title: VPC & Networking: Configuration Overview
documents.content:
### Configuration Overview

1. Go to **VPC Console → Endpoints → Create Endpoint**
2. Choose:
- **Service Type:** AWS services
- **Service Name:** e.g., S3, CloudWatch
3. Select:
- **VPC**
- **Subnet(s)** (for interface endpoint)
- **Route Table(s)** (for gateway endpoint)
4. Define **policy**, **security groups**, and **DNS settings** if needed.

documents.title: VPC & Networking: Exam Tips
documents.content:
### Exam Tips

- Only **S3** and **DynamoDB** support **Gateway Endpoints**.
- All other services use **Interface Endpoints (PrivateLink)**.
- VPC endpoints improve **security** and **performance**.
- **No need for Internet Gateway (IGW)**, **NAT Gateway**, or **VPN** to access AWS services privately.

documents.title: VPC & Networking: AWS PrivateLink
documents.content:
## AWS PrivateLink
---

documents.title: VPC & Networking: Definition
documents.content:
### Definition

AWS PrivateLink enables **private connectivity** between **VPCs**, **AWS services**, or **third-party services** **without using the public internet**.

It is part of the **VPC Endpoint Services** family.

documents.title: VPC & Networking: Purpose
documents.content:
### Purpose

- Provides **secure, private communication** over the **AWS internal network**.
- Replaces **VPC peering** for scalable, secure, and simple service sharing.
- Commonly used by **vendors (SaaS providers)** or **marketplace services** to expose applications privately to customers.

documents.title: VPC & Networking: How It Works
documents.content:
### How It Works

1. **Service Provider (Vendor side)**
- Hosts a service in their **own VPC**.
- Creates a **Network Load Balancer (NLB)** to expose the service.
- Enables it as a **VPC Endpoint Service**.
2. **Service Consumer (Customer side)**
- Creates an **Interface Endpoint (Elastic Network Interface)** in their own VPC.
- Connects privately to the vendor’s service through **PrivateLink**.
3. **Traffic Path:**
- Communication stays **within AWS’s private network** (no public internet, NAT, or VPN).

documents.title: VPC & Networking: Key Benefits
documents.content:
### Key Benefits

No exposure to the public internet
Simplified network management
Highly scalable (each new customer just creates a new endpoint)
Reduced complexity compared to VPC peering

documents.title: VPC & Networking: Exam Tips
documents.content:
### Exam Tips

- **PrivateLink** connects **VPCs privately** via **Network Load Balancers**.
- **VPC Peering** connects entire VPCs (non-scalable and not private by default).
- **PrivateLink** = secure, private access to a service across VPCs/accounts/regions.
- Traffic never leaves the **AWS internal network**.

documents.title: VPC & Networking: Hybrid Cloud Connectivity
documents.content:
## Hybrid Cloud Connectivity
---

Hybrid Cloud = Connecting **on-premises data center** with **AWS Cloud (VPC)**.
There are **two main options** for hybrid connectivity:

1. **Site-to-Site VPN**
2. **AWS Direct Connect (DX)**

documents.title: VPC & Networking: Site-to-Site VPN
documents.content:
### Site-to-Site VPN

**Definition:**
Encrypted connection between **on-premises data center** and **AWS VPC** over the **public internet**.

**Features:**

- Encrypted IPsec tunnel
- Uses **public internet**
- Quick to set up (~5 minutes)
- Lower cost, but **less reliable** and **limited bandwidth**

**Use Case:**
Temporary or quick connection setup between on-premises and AWS.

**Components:**

- **Customer Gateway (CGW):** On-premises side
- **Virtual Private Gateway (VGW):** AWS side

**Exam Tip:**
🧠 _To establish Site-to-Site VPN, you need CGW (customer) + VGW (AWS)._

documents.title: VPC & Networking: AWS Direct Connect (DX)
documents.content:
### AWS Direct Connect (DX)

**Definition:**
A **dedicated private physical connection** between **on-premises** and **AWS**.

**Features:**

- Traffic flows **over private AWS network** (not public internet)
- **High bandwidth**, **low latency**, **secure**, **reliable**
- More expensive and takes **weeks (≈1 month)** to set up
- Requires connection through **Direct Connect partner**

**Use Case:**
When you need **consistent performance**, **high data transfer**, or **private link**.

documents.title: VPC & Networking: Comparison: Site-to-Site VPN vs Direct Connect
documents.content:
### Comparison: Site-to-Site VPN vs Direct Connect

|Feature|Site-to-Site VPN|Direct Connect|
|---|---|---|
|**Connection Type**|Encrypted over Public Internet|Private Physical Connection|
|**Setup Time**|Minutes|Weeks|
|**Cost**|Low|High|
|**Speed/Bandwidth**|Limited|High|
|**Reliability**|Medium|Very High|
|**Security**|Encrypted but public|Private and secure|
|**Use Case**|Quick setup, backup|Long-term, high performance|

documents.title: VPC & Networking: 🧾 **Exam Summary**
documents.content:
### 🧾 **Exam Summary**

- Hybrid cloud = On-premises + AWS VPC
- **Site-to-Site VPN** → Fast, cheap, encrypted, public internet
- **Direct Connect (DX)** → Slow to set up, private, fast, reliable

- Choose **DX** for secure, high-performance, private connections

documents.title: VPC & Networking: AWS Client VPN
documents.content:
## AWS Client VPN
---

documents.title: VPC & Networking: Definition
documents.content:
### Definition

AWS **Client VPN** is a **managed, scalable VPN service** that allows individual **users (clients)** to securely connect from their computers to **AWS VPC** or **on-premises networks** using **OpenVPN protocol**.

documents.title: VPC & Networking: Purpose / Use Case
documents.content:
### Purpose / Use Case

- Allows a user’s **computer** to securely connect to a **private VPC** over the **public internet**.
- Enables access to **private resources** (like EC2 instances in private subnets) **using private IPs**.
- Useful for developers, admins, or remote employees who need **secure access** to internal AWS networks.

documents.title: VPC & Networking: How It Works
documents.content:
### How It Works

1. The **Client VPN software** (OpenVPN-based) is installed on the user’s computer.
2. The connection is established **over the public internet** to **AWS Client VPN endpoint**.
3. Once connected, the user’s machine behaves as if it is **inside the VPC**.
4. The user can access **EC2 instances** or other private resources **using private IPs**.
5. If the VPC is also connected to **on-premises data center** (via Site-to-Site VPN),
→ the user can securely access **on-prem servers** as well.

documents.title: VPC & Networking: Key Points for Exam
documents.content:
### Key Points for Exam

|Concept|Explanation|
|---|---|
|**Protocol Used**|OpenVPN|
|**Connection Type**|Over public internet (encrypted)|
|**Access Level**|Individual user-level (client)|
|**Main Benefit**|Secure remote access to private AWS or on-prem networks|
|**Integrates With**|VPC and optionally Site-to-Site VPN for hybrid access|

documents.title: VPC & Networking: Summary
documents.content:
### Summary

- **Site-to-Site VPN** → Connects **networks** (on-prem to AWS).
- **Client VPN** → Connects **individual users** (laptops/desktops) to AWS.
- Enables private access without exposing resources to the public internet.

documents.title: VPC & Networking: AWS Transit Gateway (TGW)
documents.content:
## AWS Transit Gateway (TGW)
---

documents.title: VPC & Networking: Definition
documents.content:
### Definition

AWS **Transit Gateway** is a **central hub** that allows you to connect **multiple VPCs**, **on-premises networks**, and **VPNs** together in a **hub-and-spoke** model.

It simplifies complex network topologies and replaces the need for multiple VPC peering connections.

documents.title: VPC & Networking: Why It Exists
documents.content:
### Why It Exists

- When you have **many VPCs** and **on-premises connections**, managing **individual peering links** and **routing tables** becomes messy.
- Transit Gateway provides a **single, centralized gateway** to manage and route traffic between all networks.

documents.title: VPC & Networking: How It Works
documents.content:
### How It Works

- All VPCs, **Direct Connect Gateways**, and **Site-to-Site VPNs** connect to **one Transit Gateway**.
- The TGW acts as a **hub**, and each VPC acts as a **spoke** in the topology.
- **No need for VPC peering** between every pair of VPCs.
- Simplifies routing and scales to **thousands of VPCs**.

documents.title: VPC & Networking: Supports
documents.content:
### Supports

Amazon VPCs
VPN connections
AWS Direct Connect Gateways
On-premises networks

documents.title: VPC & Networking: Exam Tip
documents.content:

|---|---|
|Connect 2 VPCs directly|**VPC Peering**|
|Connect On-premises to AWS over internet|**Site-to-Site VPN**|
|Connect On-premises to AWS privately|**Direct Connect**|
|Connect many VPCs and on-prem together (hub-and-spoke)|**Transit Gateway**|

documents.title: VPC & Networking: Key Benefits
documents.content:
### Key Benefits

- Centralized network management
- Scalable and simplified routing
- Integration with hybrid architectures
- Works across multiple AWS accounts

documents.title: VPC & Networking: Summary
documents.content:
### Summary

> **Transit Gateway = “Network Hub” for multi-VPC and hybrid connections**
> If you see **hundreds or thousands of VPCs + on-premises systems**, the correct answer is **Transit Gateway**.

## Amazon VPC (Virtual Private Cloud) Summary
---

documents.title: VPC & Networking: Core Concepts
documents.content:
### Core Concepts

- **VPC** stands for **Virtual Private Cloud** — your **isolated private network** within AWS.
- **Subnet**: a subdivision of your VPC, tied to a **specific Availability Zone**.

documents.title: VPC & Networking: Internet Connectivity
documents.content:
### Internet Connectivity

- To allow **internet access** → attach an **Internet Gateway (IGW)** to your VPC.
- **Private instances** (in private subnets) need a **NAT Gateway** or **NAT Instance** for outbound internet traffic.

documents.title: VPC & Networking: Firewalls
documents.content:
### Firewalls

- **Network ACL (NACL)**:
- Operates at **subnet level**.
- **Stateless** (each request and response is evaluated separately).
- Controls **inbound and outbound traffic** rules.
- **Security Groups (SGs)**:
- Operate at **instance (EC2/ENI) level**.
- **Stateful** (responses are automatically allowed).
- Control **inbound/outbound rules** for individual instances.

documents.title: VPC & Networking: Elastic IPs
documents.content:
### Elastic IPs

- Static **public IPv4** addresses.
- Incurs cost **if not attached to a running instance**.

documents.title: VPC & Networking: Connecting VPCs
documents.content:
### Connecting VPCs

- **VPC Peering**: Connects two VPCs **privately** if they have **non-overlapping CIDR blocks**.
- **Non-transitive** (A↔B and B↔C doesn’t mean A↔C).

documents.title: VPC & Networking: Private Connectivity to AWS Services
documents.content:
### Private Connectivity to AWS Services

- **VPC Endpoints**:
- Allow **private access** to AWS services (e.g., S3, DynamoDB) **without internet**.
- **AWS PrivateLink**:
- Enables **private connection** to **third-party or other VPC services** through **Network Load Balancer**.

documents.title: VPC & Networking: Network Monitoring
documents.content:
### Network Monitoring

- **VPC Flow Logs**: capture **network traffic metadata** for analysis and troubleshooting.

documents.title: VPC & Networking: Hybrid Connectivity (On-Prem ↔ AWS)
documents.content:
### Hybrid Connectivity (On-Prem ↔ AWS)

- **Site-to-Site VPN**:
- Secure IPsec connection over the **public internet** between **on-premises data center and AWS**.
- **Client VPN**:
- Lets **individual users** connect securely from their **local computers** using **OpenVPN**.
- **AWS Direct Connect**:
- Provides **dedicated private fiber connection** from **on-premises to AWS**, bypassing the internet.

documents.title: VPC & Networking: Large-Scale Connectivity
documents.content:
### Large-Scale Connectivity

- **Transit Gateway (TGW)**:
- Central hub for **connecting multiple VPCs, VPNs, and Direct Connect links**.
- Simplifies management of **thousands of connections**.

documents.title: VPC & Networking: Exam Focus
documents.content:
### Exam Focus

- Know when to use **IGW, NAT, NACL, SG, Peering, PrivateLink, VPN, Direct Connect, and TGW**.
- Understand **stateful vs stateless** firewalls.
- Recognize **private vs public** access scenarios.
- Be clear on **VPC Peering vs Transit Gateway** and **PrivateLink vs VPC Endpoint**.

documents.title: CAP Theorem
documents.content:
CAP Theorem
categories:
Read: https://ahmadx.dev/posts/cap-theorem/

documents.title: CAP Theorem
documents.content:
CAP theorem is one of those ideas everyone knows, but very few actually design with. And that’s because it’s usually taught as a formula, not as a pressure situation.

So let’s do this the system designer way.

Assume you’re building a distributed system. Not a single server, not a single database. Multiple nodes, multiple machines, talking over a network. The moment you distribute a system, one thing becomes inevitable: things will fail. Machines crash. Networks slow down. Packets get lost. You don’t get to opt out of this.

Now CAP enters the picture.

CAP talks about three guarantees your system might want:
Consistency: every read sees the latest written data
Availability: every request gets a response (not an error)
Partition tolerance: the system continues to work even if network communication breaks between nodes

Here’s the key insight most beginners miss:
Partition tolerance is not a choice in real distributed systems. Networks will fail. So the real tradeoff is never CA vs CP vs AP. In practice, it’s always Consistency vs Availability under a partition.

Let’s see what that actually means.

Imagine a distributed database with two nodes, Node A and Node B. They replicate data between them. Everything is fine until the network cable between them breaks. This is a partition. Now a user sends a write request to Node A, and another user sends a read request to Node B.

The system designer must answer one uncomfortable question:
What do we do right now?

Option 1: Favor consistency.
Node B refuses to answer reads because it might be outdated. The system returns an error or waits until the partition heals. Data stays correct, but users experience downtime. This is the CP choice.

documents.title: CAP Theorem
documents.content:
Option 2: Favor availability.
Node B answers the read using whatever data it has, even if it’s stale. The system stays responsive, but different users may see different data temporarily. This is the AP choice.

There is no third option. You can’t magically have both once the partition exists.

Now let’s ground this with intuition.

Think of a banking system. If your balance is wrong even for a second, that’s unacceptable. The system would rather say “try again later” than show incorrect data. Banking systems lean toward consistency, even if availability suffers during failures.

Now think of social media. If your like count is slightly off or a post appears a few seconds late, nobody panics. But if the app stops loading entirely, users leave instantly. These systems lean toward availability, accepting temporary inconsistency.

Same distributed reality. Different business priorities.

Another subtle point most people misunderstand:
CAP is not about normal operation. During healthy operation, systems can often appear consistent and available. CAP becomes visible only during failures. And failures are exactly when architecture matters most.

This is why CAP is not a limitation. It’s a design lens.

It forces you to ask the right questions early:
Is it worse to be wrong or to be down?
Can the business tolerate stale data?
What kind of inconsistency is acceptable, and for how long?

CAP theorem is not saying “you can only pick two forever”.
It’s saying: when things break, you must choose what you’re willing to sacrifice.

Happy designing 🖤

documents.title: Consistent Hashing
documents.content:
Consistent Hashing
How consistent hashing keeps a distributed cache stable when nodes join or leave.
Read: https://ahmadx.dev/posts/consistent-hashing/

documents.title: Consistent Hashing
documents.content:
Let's talk about consistent hashing.

Imagine you are running a cache cluster. Four nodes. Your application needs to know which node holds a given key, so it hashes the key and takes the remainder. Key hash modulo four. Node zero, node one, node two, node three. Everyone gets a home.

This works perfectly, right up until you add a fifth node.

Now every key recalculates. Modulo five instead of modulo four. Almost every key maps somewhere new. The cache goes cold in one breath, and your database takes the entire load at once. That is the problem consistent hashing exists to solve.

The naive approach asks a question that changes its own answer. Node count is an input to the hash. Change the node count and you invalidate the mapping.

Consistent hashing removes the node count from the equation entirely.

Picture a ring instead of a list. Take the hash space and wrap it into a circle, so the largest possible hash sits right next to zero. Now place each node somewhere on that circle, at its own hash position.

To find where a key belongs, hash the key and walk clockwise until you hit a node. Whatever you land on, that is the owner.

The image shows this. On the right, four nodes on a ring. Six keys scattered between them. One dashed box where a fifth node would land. Look at what that box touches: one arc, the stretch between N1 and N2. Only the keys inside that arc change hands. Add the node and k1 moves to N5. k2 through k6 do not move at all.

On the left, the numbers. Ten keys, then the same ten after the fifth node joins. With a modulo, eight of them land somewhere new. On the ring, two.

documents.title: Consistent Hashing
documents.content:
Now add a node. It lands somewhere on the ring and takes responsibility for the arc between it and the node behind it. Only the keys in that arc move. Everything else stays exactly where it was. Add a fifth node to a four node cluster and roughly one fifth of your keys relocate.

Not nearly all of them.

That is the whole idea. Moving one thing changes one thing.

But this simple ring has an uncomfortable property. Nodes are not evenly spaced. If node two lands right next to node three, node three owns a tiny sliver of the keyspace and node one owns a huge one. That is not load balancing. That is a lottery you only realize you lost after the traffic arrives.

The standard fix is virtual nodes. Instead of placing each physical node once, place it many times, at many hash positions. Node one becomes node one a hundred and fifty places around the ring. Now the arc sizes average out, and each machine ends up owning roughly its fair share.

The randomness that was a liability becomes a tool. With enough virtual nodes it follows the law of large numbers instead of the roll of a die.

Let's ground this with intuition.

Think of a taxi rank where each driver owns a stretch of road. Add a new driver and they take over a slice that used to belong to whoever was next to them. Every other driver's stretch stays the same. Now imagine a rank where every driver renegotiates with everyone the moment a new car arrives.

Same road. Very different morning.

Now think about failure. When a node dies, its arc passes to the next node clockwise. Only that arc is affected. The cluster degrades by one node's worth of capacity instead of collapsing. That matters at three in the morning far more than it matters in a design review.

So what does this cost you?

documents.title: Consistent Hashing
documents.content:
It does not give you perfect balance, only approximate balance, and the approximation depends on your virtual node count and your hash function. Adding a node is cheaper for the cache but still not free, because that one arc's worth of keys goes cold. And the rebalance happens at the moment you can least afford it.

That is why production systems often add a node and let it warm up slowly instead of rebroadcasting everything immediately.

This is also why the technique shows up where a cache miss is expensive and a rebalance is worse. Redis Cluster splits the keyspace into fixed slots rather than a ring, then moves slots between nodes. Same instinct, smaller blast radius. Cassandra uses the ring with virtual nodes more or less as described. CDNs use it to decide which edge server owns which object.

Different implementations. One question: how do we move as little as possible when the topology changes?

The real insight is not the ring. The ring is just bookkeeping. The insight is that any mapping which depends on the total number of members will break every time the membership changes. Remove that dependency and the system becomes something you can resize while it is running.

So ask yourself the next time you write a sharding function. Does this key's destination depend on how many machines we have today?

If yes, you have built the modulo problem. You will meet it the first time you scale.

Happy designing 🖤

documents.title: CSS - Cascading Style Sheets: Block VS Inline VS Inline-Block
documents.content:
## Block VS Inline VS Inline-Block

**Block Element:-** Start on a new line (occupy full width) and take-up 100% of the width by default. You can set *height*, *width*, *margin*,*padding*. **ex:** ``, ``, ``.

**Inline Element:-** Do not start on a new line and only take-up as much width as their content/required. Height and width **cannot** be set/change. **ex:** ``,``,``.

**Inline-Block Element:-** Behave like inline element(do not start on a new line). Allow setting height,width like block elements. Useful for layouts purposes without breaking the flow.**ex:** ``,`button`,``.

27. `display:` specifies how a certain HTML should be displayed. *attributes:* `block`,`inline`,`inline-block`

documents.title: CSS - Cascading Style Sheets: Position Absolute VS Position Relative
documents.content:
## Position Absolute VS Position Relative

**Position Absolute:-**
- An element with `position: absolute` is removed from the normal document flow.
- It is positioned relative to its nearest positioned ancestor (an ancestor with `position: relative`, `absolute`, or `fixed`). If no such ancestor exists, it is positioned relative to the initial containing block (viewport).
- It does not occupy space in the normal layout, allowing it to move freely within its containing block.

**Position Relative:-**
- An element with `position: relative` remains in the normal document flow.
- It is positioned relative to its **original position**, using `top`, `right`, `bottom`, and `left` values.
- Space for the element is still reserved in the layout, so it affects other elements.

28. `position:` specifies the type of positioning method used for an element `absolute`,`relative`,`fixed`.

documents.title: CSS - Cascading Style Sheets: Background Properties
documents.content:
## Background Properties

29. `background:` A shorthand property for all the background properties. It set by `img()`,`color`, `linear-gradiant(to bottom right, red,yellow)` etc.
30. `background-size:` Specifies the size of the background images like `cover`,`contain` etc.
31. `background-repeat:` Sets if/how a background image will be repeated. like `no-repeat`, `round` etc.
32. `background-position:` specifies the position of a background image like `center`,`right`, `left`,`top`,`bottom`.

documents.title: CSS - Cascading Style Sheets: Flexbox
documents.content:
## Flexbox

Flexbox is a CSS layout model designed to help arrange elements in a responsive flexible way. It simplifies alignment, distribution, and spacing of items within a container-even when their size is unknown or dynamic. The Flexbox model is one-dimensional, meaning it handles either row or a column layout, Unlike CSS Grid which is two-dimensional(rows and columns).

documents.title: CSS - Cascading Style Sheets: Key Concepts
documents.content:
### Key Concepts

- *Flex Container:* The parent element that holds flex items. We can define a flex container by applying `display: flex;` to it.
- *Flex items:* The child elements of a flex container that will be laid out according to the flexbox rules.

documents.title: CSS - Cascading Style Sheets: Main Axis and Cross Axis
documents.content:
### Main Axis and Cross Axis

- *Main Axis(x-axis):* This axis along which flex items are placed. It depends on the `flex-direction` property (row by default).
- *Cross Axis(y-axis):* The perpendicular axis to the main axis. for example, if the `flex-direction` is row, the cross axis will be vertical.

documents.title: CSS - Cascading Style Sheets: Flexbox Properties
documents.content:
### Flexbox Properties

1. `display: flex;` Defines the element as flex container.
2. `flex-direction:` Specifies the direction of the main axis like `row`, `column`,`row-reverse`,`column-reverse`.
3. `justify-content:` Aligns items along the main axis like `start`,`center`,`space-between`,`space-evenlly`.
4. `align-items:` Aligns items along the cross-axis `stretch`,`center`, `flex-start`,`flex-end`.
5. `flex-wrap:` The `flex-wrap` property specifies whether the flexible items should wrap or not. like `nowrap`,`wrap`,`wrap-reverse`.
6. `flex-shrink:` The `flex-shrink` property specifies how the item will shrink relative to the rest of the flexible items inside the same container. value like 0 or 1.

documents.title: CSS - Cascading Style Sheets: Pseudo-Class and Pseudo-Elements
documents.content:
## Pseudo-Class and Pseudo-Elements

Pseudo-elements and pseudo-classes are both powerful CSS features used to style elements based on specific states or to target parts of elements that aren't directly available in the DOM, although they serve similar purposes, modifying or styling elements based on conditions, they function differently.

documents.title: CSS - Cascading Style Sheets: Pseudo-Classes
documents.content:
### Pseudo-Classes

They targets an element in a specific state, and we use `:` for pseudo-classes.

*Syntax:* `selector:pesudo-class`

**Common Examples:**
- `:hover` when an element is hovered.
- `:focus` when an element is focused.
- `:th-child(n)` targets the nth child of parent.
- `:active` when an element is being clicked.
- `:visited` for visited links

documents.title: CSS - Cascading Style Sheets: Pseudo-Elements
documents.content:
### Pseudo-Elements

Targets part of an element or inserts content before/after it. we use `::` for elements.

*Syntax:* `selector::pesudo-element`

**Common Examples:**
- `::before` insert content before an element.
- `::after` inserts content after an element.
- `::first-letter` styles the first-letter.
- `::first-line` styles the first line.
- `::selection` styles the selected text.

| Pseudo Classes | Pseudo-Elements |
| --------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Interact with element states (e.g., :hover, :focus) | Target parts of an element or add content (e.g., ::before, ::first-letter). |

documents.title: CSS - Cascading Style Sheets: Color Science and their Units
documents.content: ## Color Science and their Units

documents.title: CSS - Cascading Style Sheets: 1. Color Name
documents.content:
### 1. Color Name

CSS provides a set of predefined names that are recognized by all browsers *ex:* `red`,`green`,`blue`,`black` (total around 140 standard names)

**Example:** `background-color: red;`

documents.title: CSS - Cascading Style Sheets: 2. Hexadecimal Notation (#RRGGBB)
documents.content:
### 2. Hexadecimal Notation (#RRGGBB)

A more precise way to specify color in CSS is using hexadecimal(hx) notation.
Hex values are written in the form #RRGGBB, where:
- #RR : represent the red component.
- #GG : represent the green component.
- #BB : represent the blue component.

The values range is `00-FF`, 00 means no color and FF means full intensity.

**Example:** `background-color: #11111b;`

documents.title: CSS - Cascading Style Sheets: 3. RGB Functional Notation
documents.content:
### 3. RGB Functional Notation

The rgb notation uses the same concept as hex but, specifies values in the decimal range from `0-255`. The format is `rgb(red,green,blue)`, where each color component is an integer between 0(no color) and 255(full intensity).

**Example:** `background-color: rgb(255,0.0);`

documents.title: CSS - Cascading Style Sheets: 4. RGBA Functional Notation
documents.content:
### 4. RGBA Functional Notation

`rgba()` extends the `rgb()` notation by adding an *alpha* channel for transparency. The format is `rgba(red,green,blue,alpha)`, where alpha value is a decimal between 0(completely transparent) and 1(completely opoque).

**Example:** `background-color: rgba(255,0,0,0.5)`.

documents.title: CSS - Cascading Style Sheets: Grid in CSS
documents.content:
## Grid in CSS

CSS Grid Layout is a powerful two-dimensional layout system designed to handle both rows and columns. It provides a way to create web layouts without relying on floats or positioning.

documents.title: CSS - Cascading Style Sheets: Core Concepts of CSS Grid
documents.content:
### Core Concepts of CSS Grid

1. **Grid Container**: The parent element where `display: grid;` is applied.
2. **Grid Items**: The direct child elements of a grid container.
3. **Grid Lines**: Horizontal and vertical lines that divide the gird into cells.

documents.title: CSS - Cascading Style Sheets: Defining a Grid
documents.content:
### Defining a Grid

- **Columns and Rows:** Use `grid-template-columns` and `grid-template-rows` to define the grid.

1. `grid-template-columns:` Specifies the size of the columns, and how many columns in a grid layout
2. `grid-template-rows:` Specifies the size of the rows in a grid layout.

- **Gap between Grid items:** Use `gap`,`row-gap`,`column-gap` to create spacing.

documents.title: CSS - Cascading Style Sheets: Alignment and Justification
documents.content:
### Alignment and Justification

1. `align-items:` Aligns items vertically inside the container.
2. `justify-items:` Aligns items horizontally inside the container.
3. `align-content:` Vertically aligns the whole grid inside the container (when total grid size is smaller than container).
4. `jusitfy-content:` Horizontally aligns the whole grid inside the container (when total grid size is smaller than container).

*Other useful properties:*

5. `justify-self:` Aligns the content for a specific grid item along the row axis
6. `align-self:` Aligns the content for a specific grid item along the column axis
7. `grid-row-start:` Specifies where to start the grid item
8. `grid-row-end:` Specifies where to end the grid item
9. `grid-column-start:` Specifies where to start the grid item
10. `grid-column-end:` Specifies where to end the grid item
11. `grid-row:` A shorthand property for the _grid-row-start_ and the _grid-row-end_ properties.*ex:* `grid-row: 1 / 3;`
12. `grid-column:` A shorthand property for the _grid-column-start_ and the _grid-column-end_ properties.*ex:* `grid-column: 1 / 4;`

documents.title: CSS - Cascading Style Sheets: CSS Grid vs Flexbox
documents.content:
### CSS Grid vs Flexbox

| **CSS Grid** | **Flexbox** |
| ---------------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| Two-dimensional layout | One-dimensional layout |
| Suitable for complex layouts | Ideal for simpler layouts (row/column) |
| Explicit rows and columns | No rows/columns concept |

documents.title: CSS - Cascading Style Sheets: Responsive Web Design
documents.content: ## Responsive Web Design

documents.title: CSS - Cascading Style Sheets: 1. Understanding Units
documents.content:
### 1. Understanding Units

The first thing in responsiveness is to understand the Absolute(like px) and Relative(em,vh) Units and given are units in css.

documents.title: CSS - Cascading Style Sheets: Absolute Units
documents.content:
#### Absolute Units

These units are fixed and not affected by the size of other elements or the viewport.

- **px (pixels):** A single pixel on the screen.
- **cm (centimeters):** A physical centimeter.
- **mm (millimeters):** A physical millimeter.
- **in (inches):** A physical inch (1 inch = 2.54 cm).

documents.title: CSS - Cascading Style Sheets: Relative Units
documents.content:
#### Relative Units

These units are based on the size of other elements, the viewport, or the font size.

documents.title: CSS - Cascading Style Sheets: Relative to the Font Size
documents.content:
##### Relative to the Font Size

- **em:** Relative to the font size of the parent element.
- **rem (root em):** Relative to the font size of the root element (``).
- **ex:** Relative to the height of the lowercase letter "x" in the current font.
- **ch:** Relative to the width of the character "0" (zero) in the current font.

documents.title: CSS - Cascading Style Sheets: Relative to the Viewport
documents.content:
##### Relative to the Viewport

- **vw (viewport width):** 1% of the viewport's width.
- **vh (viewport height):** 1% of the viewport's height.
- **vmin:** 1% of the smaller dimension (width or height) of the viewport.
- **vmax:** 1% of the larger dimension (width or height) of the viewport.

documents.title: CSS - Cascading Style Sheets: Relative to the Element's Size
documents.content:
##### Relative to the Element's Size

- **% (percentage):** Relative to the size of the parent element.

documents.title: CSS - Cascading Style Sheets: 2. Flexbox for Responsive Design
documents.content:
### 2. Flexbox for Responsive Design

Flexbox is a powerful tool for creating responsive layouts that adapt to different screen sizes and devices. Below are key takeaways for using Flexbox in responsive design:

documents.title: CSS - Cascading Style Sheets: General Concepts
documents.content:
#### General Concepts

1. **Flex Direction:**
- Use `flex-direction: row;` for horizontal layouts.
- Switch to `flex-direction: column;` for vertical layouts on smaller screens using media queries.
2. **Flex Wrap:**
- Use `flex-wrap: wrap;` to allow flex items to wrap onto new lines if necessary.
3. **Flex Property:**
- Use the `flex` property with percentages (e.g., `flex: 50%;`) to adjust the width of items based on the screen size.

documents.title: CSS - Cascading Style Sheets: 3. CSS Media Queries
documents.content:
### 3. CSS Media Queries

Media query is a CSS technique introduced in CSS3. It uses the `@media`rule to include a block of CSS properties only if a certain condition is true.

documents.content:

If the browser window is 600px or smaller, the background color will be lightblue:

documents.content:

Earlier in this tutorial we made a web page with rows and columns, and it was responsive, but it did not look good on a small screen.

Media queries can help with that. We can add a breakpoint where certain parts of the design will behave differently on each side of the breakpoint.

documents.title: CSS - Cascading Style Sheets: Always Design for Mobile First
documents.content:

This means that we must make some changes in our CSS.

Instead of changing styles when the width gets _smaller_ than 768px, we should change the design when the width gets _larger_ than 768px. This will make our design Mobile First:

documents.content:

There are tons of screens and devices with different heights and widths, so it is hard to create an exact breakpoint for each device. To keep things simple you could target five groups:

documents.title: CSS - Cascading Style Sheets: CSS Animations
documents.content:
## CSS Animations

- CSS allows animation of HTML elements without using JavaScript!.
- An animation lets an element gradually change from one style to another.
- You can change as many CSS properties you want, as many times as you want.
- To use CSS animation, you must first specify some keyframes for the animation.
- Keyframes hold what styles the element will have at certain times.
- Animations is just transaction from initial to final position.

documents.title: CSS - Cascading Style Sheets: The @keyframes Rule
documents.content:
### The @keyframes Rule

When you specify CSS styles inside the `@keyframes` rule, the animation will gradually change from the current to the new style at certain times.

documents.title: CSS - Cascading Style Sheets: CSS Animation Properties
documents.content:
### CSS Animation Properties

| Property | Description |
| ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| @keyframes | Specifies the animation code |
| animation | A shorthand property for setting all the animation properties. `animation: example 5s linear 2s infinite alternate;` |
| animation-delay | specifies a delay for start of an animation. like `1s`,`5s` |
| animation-direction | Specifies whether an animation should be played forwards, backward or in alternate cycles.`normal`,`reverse`,`alternate`,`alternate-reverse`. |
| animation-duration | specifies how long time an animation should take to complete one cycle like. `2s`,`4s`. |
| animation-iteration-count | Specifies the number of times an animation should be played. like `2`,`4`, or `infinite`. |
| animation-name | Specifies the name of the @keyframes animation. |
| animation-fill-mode | Specifies a style for the element when animation is not playing or completed(before it starts, after it ends, or both).`none`,`forwards`,`backwards`,`both`. |
| animation-timing-function | Specifes the speed curve of the animation like `ease`,`linear`,`ease-in`,`ease-out`,`ease-in-out`,`cubic-bezier(n,n,n,n)` |

documents.title: CSS - Cascading Style Sheets: Animation Timing Function
documents.content:
### Animation Timing Function

- `ease` - Specifies an animation with a slow start, then fast, then end slowly (this is default)
- `linear` - Specifies an animation with the same speed from start to end
- `ease-in` - Specifies an animation with a slow start
- `ease-out` - Specifies an animation with a slow end
- `ease-in-out` - Specifies an animation with a slow start and end
- `cubic-bezier(n,n,n,n)` - Lets you define your own values in a cubic-bezier function.

documents.title: DNS (Domain Name System)
documents.content:
DNS (Domain Name System)
How a domain name becomes an IP address, and why DNS is really a hierarchy of delegations and caches with a TTL attached.
Read: https://ahmadx.dev/posts/dns-domain-name-system/

documents.title: DNS (Domain Name System)
documents.content:
Let's talk about DNS.

Most people learn it as the phone book of the internet. You look up a name, you get a number. That metaphor is true and useless. A phone book is one book, owned by one company, updated on a schedule. DNS is a few million servers that have never met. They agree on who answers for which name.

So start where the user starts. You type ahmadx.dev and press enter. Your browser has no idea where that is. It has a name. The network only understands addresses.

Ask the uncomfortable question. Who tells the browser where to go? And who decided that server has the right to answer?

Now look at the image. Top panel, left to right.

Step one is your browser. More precisely, its stub resolver: the thin client on your machine. It knows almost nothing. Its only job is to hand the question to someone who does.

Step two is that someone. The recursive resolver. Your ISP runs one. So does Google at 8.8.8.8, and Cloudflare at 1.1.1.1. This is the only component in the picture doing real work, and it is the one you never see.

Step three is a root server. The root zone is tiny. It does not know where ahmadx.dev lives. It knows which servers are responsible for .dev, and it says so.

Step four is a TLD server. Run by the registry that owns .dev. It also does not know your address. It knows which nameservers are authoritative for ahmadx.dev.

Step five is the authoritative nameserver. Yours might be your registrar, your DNS host, or a cloud provider. This is the only server that can actually answer. It returns the record. In my case, an A record pointing at 216.198.79.1, with a TTL of 1800 seconds.

Now notice what steps three and four did. They did not answer. They referred. Each handed back a smaller question, not a result, and the resolver followed the chain.

documents.title: DNS (Domain Name System)
documents.content:
That is the whole architecture: a hierarchy of delegation, with one willing worker at the top of the tree doing the walking.

Bottom left panel. Recursive versus iterative.

Recursive is the contract between you and the resolver: ask once, get a final answer or an error. Iterative is the contract between the resolver and everyone else: each authority hands back a referral, and the resolver keeps asking.

Get these two backwards and half of DNS stops making sense.

Bottom middle panel. Record types.

An A record is an IPv4 address. AAAA is IPv6. CNAME says this name is an alias for that name, so the resolver chases it again. MX says where mail goes, and carries a priority. TXT carries arbitrary text, which is why SPF, DKIM and domain verification all live there. NS says who is authoritative for a zone, and the whole delegation chain hangs from it.

One name, many records. The type decides the meaning.

There is one trap at the apex: you cannot put a CNAME there. ahmadx.dev cannot be an alias, only www.ahmadx.dev can. The apex needs NS and SOA records, and a CNAME would collide with them.

Bottom right panel. TTL.

An answer is a lease, not a fact. When the authoritative server replies, it attaches a number of seconds. Every resolver in the chain may keep that answer for exactly that long, then must ask again.

This is why "DNS propagation" is a misleading phrase. Nothing propagates. Old answers simply expire at different times on different caches. Your record changed in one second. The world catches up over one TTL.

Which gives you a practical rule: lower the TTL before a migration, and do it a full old-TTL ahead of the change. Otherwise you sit there for a day waiting on a cache you cannot reach, arguing with a customer who can.

documents.title: DNS (Domain Name System)
documents.content:
But do not romanticize DNS either. It is not a load balancer. Round robin A records look like balancing until a client caches one address and never moves. It is not a failover mechanism either: health checks at the authoritative server only help clients that ask again. And every shortcut you take with TTL, you pay for in query volume at the exact moment your servers are least able to take it.

There is also a layer most people skip. DNSSEC signs records so a resolver can check the answer came from the zone that owns it. It does not encrypt anything. Anyone on the path still sees which names you ask for.

So here is the mental model: DNS is a distributed cache with a slow, hierarchical way of filling itself. Delegation decides who may answer. TTL decides how long anyone believes it.

Let me leave you with one question. The next time a record change "takes time to propagate" in your team, do you know which cache is still holding the old answer? If not, you are debugging by waiting.

Happy designing 🖤

documents.title: DOM Manipulation in JavaScript
documents.content:
DOM Manipulation in JavaScript
Learn how to manipulate the DOM (Document Object Model) in JavaScript by selecting, creating, and removing elements dynamically. Understand the differences between innerHTML, innerText, and textContent.
Read: https://ahmadx.dev/posts/dom-js/

documents.title: DOM Manipulation in JavaScript: DOM Manipulation in JavaScript
documents.content:
# DOM Manipulation in JavaScript

DOM (Document Object Model) Manipulation in JavaScript refers to **modifying HTML elements dynamically** using JavaScript. This includes **selecting, modifying, adding, or removing elements** from the webpage.

documents.title: DOM Manipulation in JavaScript: Selecting Elements in the DOM
documents.content:
## Selecting Elements in the DOM

Before modifying elements, we need to **select** them. Here are the different ways:

|**Method**|**Description**|**Example**|
|---|---|---|
|`document.getElementById(id)`|Selects an element by its **ID**|`document.getElementById("myDiv")`|
|`document.getElementsByClassName(className)`|Selects elements by **class name** (returns an HTMLCollection)|`document.getElementsByClassName("myClass")`|
|`document.getElementsByTagName(tagName)`|Selects elements by **tag name** (returns an HTMLCollection)|`document.getElementsByTagName("p")`|
|`document.querySelector(selector)`|Selects **the first** element that matches the CSS selector|`document.querySelector(".myClass")`|
|`document.querySelectorAll(selector)`|Selects **all** elements that match the CSS selector (returns a NodeList)|`document.querySelectorAll("div")`|

documents.content: ## Examples of Selection Methods

documents.content: ### 1. Selecting an Element by ID

documents.title: DOM Manipulation in JavaScript: 2. Selecting Elements by Class Name
documents.content: ### 2. Selecting Elements by Class Name

documents.title: DOM Manipulation in JavaScript: 3. Selecting Elements by Tag Name
documents.content: ### 3. Selecting Elements by Tag Name

documents.content:
